study.title: 2 Kings 2 The translation of Elijah and the confirmation of Elisha's ministry
study.overview: The chapter narrates the solemn passage of Elijah's prophetic ministry to Elisha. Elijah travels with Elisha a final journey, testing his firmness and preparing the succession. In the Jordan, God authenticates the new prophet with the same sign that accompanied Elijah: the waters open. Then Elijah is taken to heaven in a whirlpool, and Elisha receives the robe from his master, a sign of continuity of vocation and authority. Then the text shows Elisha recognized by the sons of the prophets, rejecting an unnecessary search for Elijah, purifying the waters of Jericho and exercising judgment on the scoffers at Bethel. The chapter ends with Elisha returning to Samaria, already acting publicly as a prophet instead of Elijah.

outline.title: The last walk of Elijah with Elisha
outline.explanation: Elijah follows from Gilgal to Bethel, Jericho and to the Jordan, always accompanied by Elisha, who refuses to stay behind. The sons of the prophets already know that the departure of Elijah is near, and the insistence of Elisha shows allegiance and determination to remain to the end.

outline.title: The crossing of the Jordan and the ascension of Elijah
outline.explanation: Elijah injures the waters with his robe, the river opens, and he offers Elisha the opportunity to ask whatever he wants before his departure. Elisha asks for a double portion of the spirit of Elijah, that is, the successor's own inheritance; soon afterward, Elijah ascends to heaven in a whirlpool, while Elisha laments his loss.

outline.title: Elisha receives the robe and is recognized
outline.explanation: Elisha takes the mantle that fell from Elijah, repeats the sign on the Jordan and crosses the waters, demonstrating that God enables him as successor. The sons of the prophets recognize that the spirit of Elijah rests upon him. When they insist on seeking Elijah, Elisha warns them, and the search ends without result.

outline.title: Miracles in Jericho and Judgment in Bethel
outline.explanation: In Jericho, Elisha heals the evil waters through salt and declares that the LORD removes death and sterility from that fountain. At Bethel, some young men ridicule him, mocking his authority and his connection with the ascension of Elijah; Elisha curses them in the name of the LORD, and two bears attack them. The chapter closes with Elisha going to Carmel and then returning to Samaria.

study.context: The text places the scene in cities linked to the prophetic path of Elijah and Elisha - Gilgal, Bethel, Jericho, the Jordan, Carmel and Samaria - without providing other historical details beyond what the chapter itself narrates. The children of the prophets appear as groups linked to teaching and observing the prophetic ministry. The chapter also presupposes that the departure of Elijah was already awaited by this prophetic circle.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes God's sovereignty over life, mission and ministerial succession. Elijah does not disappear by chance; the LORD takes him. The continuity of the ministry does not depend on the physical presence of the previous prophet, but on the Spirit of God resting on the successor. The mantle functions as a visible sign of call and transfer of office, but the power is in God, not in the object itself. The opening of the Jordan echoes the divine action in favor of its people and authenticates the new prophet. At the same time, the text shows that the prophetic word brings grace and judgment: heals the waters of Jericho and condemns the irreverent mockery in Bethel. Elisha's stance unites dependence, fidelity and authority received, not produced on his own merit.

scholarViews.insight: Elijah's going to heaven transfers the prophetic mantle to Elisha, that is, the external sign of ministerial succession.
Elisha's insistence not to abandon Elijah shows constancy of affection and accompaniment until the end of the journey.
The request for a doubled portion is not material ambition, but requested by the spiritual inheritance of the first heir, that is, the continuation of Elijah's prophetic influence in Elisha.

questions: What does Elisha's faithfulness, when he not forsake Elijah, teaches about perseverance in the call of God?
How does Elisha's request for a double portion help us to understand spiritual dependence, not personal ambition?
How does this chapter show that true ministry is confirmed by God's action, and not just by external signs or human recognition?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to remain faithful to the received call, even when there are transitions, losses and uncertainties. It also teaches to value God's work in the succession of spiritual leadership, without carnal attachment to the previous messenger. In practice, this implies honoring faithful service, seeking the Lord before seeking quick answers, and dealing with reverence what God has established. The concrete application today is: persevering in obedience, asking God to enable it to serve, and avoid mockery against what He sanctifies.
study.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty in the exact scope of terms translated as "boys" in 2:23, as the notes indicate that the term can cover young people of a wider age, perhaps even almost adult boys. It is also not possible to affirm accurately, from the notes provided, as from the 2:11 scene should be described in detail beyond what the text says: Elijah's translation is clearly God's work, but the comments vary in the way they describe their immediate aspects.
